# Results — Study 470 (Stochastic Momentum Index)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The believers' claim — **the SMI
times turns: when it rises up out of oversold, a bounce follows** — encoded as a mechanical rule.
The SMI is Blau's double-smoothed range oscillator (N = 13, s1 = 25, s2 = 2), bounded ±100; a long
fires when the SMI was below −40 on the prior bar and turns up, entered at the **next close** (one
documented lag), and we measure the forward 5/10/20/60-day return. Offline & deterministic once
cached; run `python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily adjusted (**total-return**) closes for **SPY, QQQ, IWM, DIA, GLD** (public, no key) |
| Window | 2005-01-03 → 2026-05-29 (**As-of 2026-05-31**, partial June dropped; **21.4** years) |
| SPY fingerprint | `4cb5244f3990` (sha1[:12] of the close column, As-of slice) |
| Indicator | SMI N = 13, s1 = 25, s2 = 2; oversold gate −40; bounded ±100 |
| Entries | **226** mechanical "SMI rising out of oversold" turns pooled across the 5 tapes |
| Timing / costs | SMI is causal; turn read on close of *t*; enter the **next close** (one lag); hold 5/10/20/60 days; **1 bp** one-way × 2 legs per turn |

> **Price-only vs total-return.** The ETFs are auto-adjusted (dividends reinvested) — labelled
> total-return everywhere. The Signal axis uses a basket of **surviving** liquid ETFs; this is a
> single-instrument timing study, not a cross-sectional anomaly, so survivorship affects only the
> drift baseline (which is exactly what the random-entry control neutralizes).

## The signal — SMI-turn vs a drift-matched random baseline (the honest test)

One-sample *t* is the **misleading** number (it measures the index's upward drift); the
**Welch turn-vs-random** *t* is the test that matters. The random baseline is a **large** draw
(1000 dates/ticker) so it is a *stable* estimate of the tape's true drift — important because the
turn entries are sparse (226). Δ = turn − random.

| horizon | n | turn | win% | one-sample *t* | random | Δ (turn−random) | net of cost | Welch *t* | *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 5-day  | 226 | +72.2 bps  | 65% | +3.40 | +20.9 bps  | **+51.3 bps**  | +70.2 bps  | **+2.34** | 0.020 |
| 10-day | 226 | +135.3 bps | 68% | +4.92 | +58.1 bps  | **+77.2 bps**  | +133.3 bps | **+2.52** | 0.013 |
| 20-day | 226 | +200.5 bps | 66% | +5.62 | +98.2 bps  | **+102.3 bps** | +198.5 bps | **+2.66** | 0.008 |
| 60-day | 221 | +393.1 bps | 69% | +4.31 | +282.7 bps | **+110.5 bps** | +391.1 bps | +1.56 | 0.120 |

Read it carefully. The one-sample *t* against zero (e.g. **+5.62** at 20d) is the usual beta — but
this time, **against the drift-matched random baseline the SMI-turn survives**. The single-seed
Welch *t* shown above (seed = 7) is +2.34 / +2.52 / +2.66 at 5/10/20d — but a single random-baseline
seed can throw a lucky *t* > 2 that isn't a real edge, so the legitimate test is seed-robustness
(next section).

## Seed-robustness of the turn-vs-random Welch *t* — the test that actually decides "Real"

A single drift-matched baseline draw is one sample of the tape's drift; a lucky seed can inflate the
Welch *t* above 2 with no real edge underneath (Study 452 was caught exactly this way). So we
re-draw the random baseline over **20 seeds** (n = 1000/ticker each) and report the **mean**, the
**spread (min/max)**, and the **fraction of seeds clearing *t* ≥ 2**. The turn returns are
seed-free; only the baseline re-draws.

| horizon | seed-avg Welch *t* | min | max | frac of seeds *t* ≥ 2 | robust? |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|:--:|
| 5-day  | **+2.22** | +1.70 | +2.91 | 0.70 | borderline |
| 10-day | **+2.84** | +2.33 | +3.25 | **1.00** | **yes** |
| 20-day | **+2.71** | +2.10 | +3.25 | **1.00** | **yes** |
| 60-day | +1.38 | +0.87 | +2.06 | 0.05 | no |

This is the decisive number, and it is **not** a seed-luck artifact. At **10 and 20 days every one
of the 20 seeds clears *t* ≥ 2** (min +2.33 / +2.10), and the seed-averaged *t* is +2.84 / +2.71 —
*above* the lucky seed = 7 values, not below them. (Pushing the baseline draw to n = 10 000 removes
the sampling noise entirely and the Welch *t* converges to +2.18 / +2.83 / +2.68 at 5/10/20d.) The
**5-day** horizon is genuinely weaker: seed = 7 gave +2.34 but the seed-averaged *t* is +2.22 and
only 70% of seeds clear 2, so 5d is *borderline* and the Real stamp rests on the robust **10/20-day**
horizons. At 60 days the gap is positive but never significant. So, unlike most technical rules on
this desk, the SMI-turn does **robustly beat random** at the 10- and 20-day horizons — a genuine, if
modest, signal.

## Structure placebo — destroy the SMI's geometry, the edge vanishes

The cleanest "is it the *structure* or just the drift?" test: keep the tape, the epoch and the
**exact per-ticker number of entries**, but place those entries on **random dates** (destroying the
SMI's defining "rising out of oversold" geometry). If the structure carries the signal, the real
turn must sit far in the right tail.

| horizon | observed turn | placebo *p* | beats / draws |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 5-day  | +72.2 bps  | **0.0033** | 0 / 300 |
| 10-day | +135.3 bps | **0.0033** | 0 / 300 |
| 20-day | +200.5 bps | **0.0033** | 0 / 300 |

**Zero of 300** count-matched random-date placebos match the real SMI turn at any horizon
(*p* = 0.0033) — the SMI-turn *structure*, not the tape's drift, is doing the work. (This is distinct
from the *parameter* placebo below, which scrambles Blau's specific tuning and does *not* reject —
i.e. the structure is load-bearing but Blau's exact (13, 25, 2) is not.)

## Per-ticker (H = 20) — positive delta in all five names

| ticker | entries | turn | one-sample *t* | random | Δ (turn−random) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY | 32 | +227.5 bps | +3.37 | +88.8 bps  | **+138.6 bps** |
| QQQ | 45 | +144.1 bps | +1.11 | +122.0 bps | **+22.1 bps**  |
| IWM | 49 | +281.8 bps | +3.94 | +90.3 bps  | **+191.5 bps** |
| DIA | 38 | +219.9 bps | +3.82 | +78.3 bps  | **+141.6 bps** |
| GLD | 62 | +151.3 bps | +2.81 | +111.5 bps | **+39.9 bps**  |

The turn-minus-random delta is **positive in all 5 names** (a coherent direction, unusual for this
desk) — but it is *thin* in QQQ (+22 bps) and GLD (+40 bps), and the whole study rests on only
**226 turns over 21 years** (~2 per ticker per year). A real but sparse, fragile edge.

## Parameter placebo — scramble the SMI's tuning, nothing changes

The decisive "does *this specific* SMI matter?" test: recompute the SMI with the look-back and the
two smoothing lengths randomly perturbed away from Blau's (13, 25, 2), keeping the same *family* of
double-smoothed range oscillator on the same tape. If Blau's specific geometry forecasts turns, the
real SMI should beat the scrambled cousins.

| test | observed turn 20d return | placebo *p* | draws |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY scrambled-parameter SMI | +227.5 bps | **0.419** | 500 |

**42% of scrambled-parameter oscillators match or beat the real Blau SMI** (*p* = 0.419). The
signal is **not** about Blau's specific tuning — any "buy a smoothed oversold dip" oscillator of the
same family does just as well. The edge is the *oversold-mean-reversion family*, not the SMI.

## Synthetic positive control — the harness CAN bank a real bounce

On a deterministic tape with a *planted* oversold bounce (knob `edge`, keyed off the same causal
SMI the rule reads), the same turn rule behaves exactly as it must — so the real-tape signal is a
genuine detection, not an artefact, and the edge=0 fair-coin proves there is no false positive.

| planted edge | n | turn | win% | one-sample *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **0.00** (no bounce) | 54 | +68.7 bps | 63% | +0.75 |
| **0.60** (real planted bounce) | 50 | +190.1 bps | 70% | **+2.56** |

With no planted bounce the control sits at *t* ≈ 0.75 (no false positive — the residual is drift); a
real planted bounce lights up at *t* = +2.56 with a 70% win-rate. The detector is live.

## Verdict

- **Signal — REAL.** The "SMI rising out of oversold" turn **robustly beats** a drift-matched random
  baseline at the desk's *t* ≥ 2 bar on the **10- and 20-day** horizons — and crucially this is
  *seed-robust*: averaging the turn-vs-random Welch *t* over 20 baseline seeds gives **+2.84 / +2.71**
  with **every** seed clearing 2 (min +2.33 / +2.10), not a lucky single-seed throw (it converges to
  +2.83 / +2.68 as the baseline draw grows). The 5-day horizon is weaker (seed-avg *t* = +2.22, only
  70% of seeds ≥ 2 — borderline). The turn-minus-random delta (Δ = +77 / +102 bps at 10/20d) is
  positive in **all five** names, and the **structure placebo rejects hard** — count-matched
  random-date entries beat the real turn in **0 of 300** draws (*p* = 0.0033). This is not pure beta:
  the gap survives both the random-entry control and the structure placebo. (At 60 days the gap is
  positive but never significant, seed-avg *t* = +1.38.)
- **Tradability — FRAGILE.** The edge is real but **thin and sparse**: only 226 turns in 21 years
  (~2/ticker/year), the delta is small in 2 of 5 names, it fades by 60 days, and — decisively — the
  parameter placebo shows it is **not** the specific Blau SMI but the generic oversold-dip family
  doing the work (*p* = 0.42). Tiny trade count + parameter-agnostic + horizon-sensitive = fragile,
  not investable. You would not deploy *this* indicator on this evidence; you would test the broader
  short-horizon oversold-reversion effect with far more data.
- **"Does the SMI forecast turns"? — MIXED.** The oversold turn genuinely precedes above-drift
  bounces (confirmed at short horizons), so *something* real is there. But the parameter scramble
  shows it is **not Blau's specific SMI** doing the forecasting — any double-smoothed oversold
  oscillator works equally well. The claim "the *SMI* times turns" is therefore half right: a
  short-horizon oversold-reversion effect exists, but the credit does not belong to this particular
  indicator's special construction.
